I woke up before the alarm again, which feels like a small betrayal and a small kindness all at once. The ceiling is white and cracked in a way I have memorized without meaning to memorize it. Somewhere a pipe knocks. Somewhere a bird is practicing the same three notes over and over, as if music could be built from repetition alone, as if trying again is enough.

I do not get up right away. I let the light come in sideways through the blinds and make stripes across the blanket. Dust lives in that light, turning slowly, gold and grey at the same time. I think about how many mornings I have wasted by thinking about wasting them, which is a different kind of waste, more efficient, more honest. The coffee from yesterday is still on the nightstand.

When I finally stand, my feet are cold. The floor remembers the night. I pad to the kitchen and pour too much water into the kettle because I am thinking about something else, something I have forgotten to remember on purpose. It makes a sound like a distant train. I watch the window fill with fog, and in the fog I see a version of myself that is younger, holding a mug with both hands, not knowing yet what the next ten years will ask of him.

Outside, the street is quiet enough to hear the bins being rolled to the curb. One lid clatters. One dog barks once, thoughtfully, as if it has decided something. I open the back door a crack and let the cold in to balance the kettle's heat. The air smells of wet leaves and somebody else's woodsmoke, and for a moment I am twelve again, walking home from school in January, my coat too big, my pockets full of stones I intended to keep forever.

I still have some of those stones, I think, in a drawer with dead batteries and rubber bands that have fused into a single rubber creature. Memory is a terrible archivist. It keeps the smell of a classroom and throws away the face of the teacher. It keeps the exact weight of a jacket in the rain and loses the words to a song I loved for a whole summer. Maybe that is mercy. Maybe that is just how the brain edits, cutting until only the feeling remains, bright and unexplainable and true in the way dreams are true.

The kettle clicks off. I make coffee strong enough to stand a spoon in, as my grandfather used to say, although I do not think he ever actually did that, and I do not think I ever will. The first sip burns my tongue and resets something small and important. I sit at the table that wobbles on one leg and I do not fix it. I have learned to eat around the wobble, to hold the mug with one hand on the edge. It is a minor skill, but it is mine.

There is a plant on the windowsill that I have not killed yet, which feels like a moderate triumph. It leans toward the light with a kind of desperate optimism I admire and do not share. I water it and talk to it a little, not because I believe in that, but because talking changes the air in the room somehow. It makes the morning less empty. The plant does not answer, but the quiet after I speak is different from the quiet before, and that difference is something.

I check my phone, which is a habit I perform the way other people bite their nails. Nothing urgent. A message from a friend in a city I have never visited, a photograph of a cat sitting on a keyboard, an invitation to something I will probably not attend. I read it twice and put the phone face down. The cat looks judgmental, and maybe it is right to look that way. We are all typing on the keyboards of our lives while cats walk across them, indifferent and perfect and utterly necessary.

Later, I will walk to the shops and buy bread and milk and one thing I do not need, because a small unnecessary thing makes the day feel chosen rather than endured. I will nod to the woman at the till who always asks if I have found everything, and I will say yes, even if I have not, because finding everything is not really the point. On the way home the sun will be higher and the street will be louder, and someone will be laughing on a balcony, and I will think, without bitterness, that happiness is mostly a matter of being in the right light at the right time.

But that is later. Right now the coffee is warm and the plant is leaning and the house is ticking in its sleep. I could write a list of everything I intend to do today, and I probably will, and I will cross some of it off with a satisfying line, and I will leave the rest for tomorrow, where it will wait with great patience. Time is kinder than we think when we stop arguing with it. It just keeps going, stone by stone, morning by morning, building something none of us planned.

So I sit a little longer, watching the dust turn in the light, listening to the bird that will not learn a new song because the old one is good enough, and I let the day begin without rushing to meet it halfway. Whatever comes next, comes next. I am here, and the coffee is warm, and that is a beginning as honest as any other, and it does not need to be more than that to be enough for now, for this morning, for this one small and numbered day among all the others still waiting in line.

And the light keeps changing, and I keep watching. Still here.
